Observation: Revenue is growing, but growth is slowing
Business Implication (interpretation): Forecasting should model trend plus seasonality; the slowdown is worth diagnosing (fewer new customers or lower frequency?)

Observation: October is the peak month every year; Oct-Dec are always above average
Business Implication (interpretation): Plan inventory, staffing and marketing budget around the festive quarter

Observation: The festive peak is the least profitable month
Business Implication (interpretation): Festive growth is being bought with discounts; review the depth of festive discounts on thin-margin items

Observation: Electronics dominates revenue but not profit
Evidence: Electronics = 50.1% of revenue, 23.3% of profit, margin 10.9%
Business Implication (interpretation): Revenue KPIs alone overstate Electronics' contribution; judge categories on profit

Observation: Fashion is the profit engine, but has the highest return rate
Evidence: Fashion = 20.1% of revenue, 36.8% of profit (margin 42.8%); return rate 10.9% vs 4.1% max elsewhere
Business Implication (interpretation): Reducing Fashion returns (sizing guides, fit tools) could protect the highest-margin revenue

Observation: Some top-selling items barely break even or lose money
Evidence: 43-inch 4K Smart TV: revenue ₹24.98 L, profit -₹41,713 (margin -1.7%); AeroBook Pro 16 margin 2.2%; loss-making lines = 249 (9.7% of revenue)
Business Implication (interpretation): Review pricing, supplier cost and discount caps for these SKUs

Observation: Deeper discounts go with lower margins in every category, while quantity barely changes
Evidence: Within-category Spearman rho(discount, margin): -0.89 to -0.37; rho(discount, quantity) = 0.06
Business Implication (interpretation): Discounts appear to cost margin without clearly lifting volume; test targeted rather than blanket discounts (association, not causation)

Observation: The overall discount-margin table is misleading because of category mix
Evidence: Margin by bucket (all categories): 0% 29.3%, 5-10% 19.4%, 15-20% 21.6%, 25-30% 21.4%, 35-40% 20.4%; the 5-10% bucket is heavy in low-margin Electronics
Business Implication (interpretation): Always compare discount effects within a category (Simpson's paradox)

Observation: Revenue is concentrated in a minority of customers
Business Implication (interpretation): Losing a few top customers would hurt disproportionately; they are the priority for retention (RFM/CLV in Steps 5-7)

Evidence: Customers with 11+ orders: 16.2% of buyers, 52.1% of revenue; customer revenue vs order count Spearman rho = 0.842
Business Implication (interpretation): Growing purchase frequency is a stronger lever than acquiring one-off buyers

Observation: A large share of customers has gone quiet
Evidence: 688 of 1984 buyers (34.7%) have not bought in over 180 days
Business Implication (interpretation): Reactivation candidates to size in RFM (Step 5); descriptive only here

Observation: Age is linked to spend; gender and region are not
Evidence: Median customer revenue: 35-49 ₹22,012 vs 18-24 ₹9,023 (Kruskal-Wallis p<0.001); gender p=0.81, region p=0.42
Business Implication (interpretation): Age band is a candidate feature for prediction; gender/region-based targeting has little support

Observation: South leads; East grows fastest; Central's share is shrinking
Evidence: South 27.0% of revenue; East CAGR 52.9%; Central share 14.1% -> 12.7%
Business Implication (interpretation): Protect the South, invest behind East's momentum, and investigate Central's slower growth

Observation: 9.4% of booked sales never became revenue
Evidence: Lost to cancellations and returns: ₹62.55 L; COD cancel rate 6.2% vs UPI 3.5%
Business Implication (interpretation): Nudging COD users to prepaid methods could reduce leakage

Evidence: Revenue per calendar day: Saturday 1.16x and Monday 0.89x the average day
Business Implication (interpretation): Schedule campaigns and flash sales for Friday-Sunday
